props.title: The Triplets of Belleville
props.initialSlug: Grandma cycles across seas to save kidnapped cyclist

sections.content: The Triplets of Belleville revolutionized adult animation with its grotesque-yet-gorgeous visual style and nearly dialogue-free storytelling. Director Sylvain Chomet crafted a surreal love letter to French culture and jazz-age entertainment that stands uniquely apart from both Disney's polish and Japan's anime aesthetics. The film's distinctive character designs - with exaggerated proportions and rubbery movements - drew inspiration from early 20th century cartoonists like Albert Dubout, creating a world that feels both nostalgic and otherworldly.

sections.content: Chomet's film kicked open doors for more experimental adult animation in the West. Its success paved the way for works like Mary and Max (2009) and Loving Vincent (2017), proving audiences would embrace animation that tackled mature themes with sophisticated visual approaches. The film's minimal dialogue approach also influenced later works like Wall-E (2008), demonstrating how animation could tell complex emotional stories through pure visual storytelling.

The film's jazz-infused soundtrack and 1930s setting connects it to a broader tradition of French films celebrating their musical heritage, from Django (2017) to Paris Blues (1961). But Chomet twists these familiar elements into something uniquely bizarre, with the titular elderly jazz singers performing percussion with household items in a way that feels both authentic to the era and delightfully absurd. sections.content: The film's technical achievements were groundbreaking for 2003, combining traditional hand-drawn animation with subtle computer assistance in a way that maintained its handcrafted feel while allowing for complex sequences. This hybrid approach influenced later films like Song of the Sea (2014) and The Secret of Kells (2009), showing how traditional animation could evolve without losing its artistic soul. The character animation, particularly in crowd scenes and the Tour de France sequences, demonstrates an almost choreographic attention to movement that rivals the work of animation masters like Miyazaki.
